content: The concept of Tomacco originated as a fictional hybrid fruit, half tomato and half tobacco, featured in the 1999 episode E-I-E-I-(Annoyed Grunt) of The Simpsons. The method of creating tomacco in the episode was entirely fictional. However, in 2003, a real-life version of tomacco was successfully produced. This hybrid is one of the rare instances where a made-up word from The Simpsons inspired a real-world application. In the Simpsons episode, Homer Simpson accidentally created tomacco by planting a mix of various seeds and fertilizing his tomato and tobacco fields with plutonium. The resulting fruit appeared to be a tomato but contained a dried, gray tobacco-like center. Despite being described as tasting terrible by several characters (e.g., Ralph Wiggum: Eww, Daddy, this tastes like Grandma. and Clancy Wiggum: My God, it DOES taste like Grandma.), the fruit was highly addictive. Homer named the creation Tomacco and began selling it in large quantities to unsuspecting buyers. The fictional cigarette company Laramie saw an opportunity to market tomacco to children legally and offered Homer $150 million for the rights. Homer refused, demanding $150 billion instead, which the executives rejected. The addictive nature of the hybrid plant was so potent that farm animals developed the ability to speak and walk on two legs in their desperate attempts to obtain more tomacco. In one instance, a cow broke through the wall of the Simpson farmhouse and screamed TOMACCO. while searching for the fruit. Eventually, all but one tomacco plant were consumed by the farm animals. The remaining plant was stolen by the Laramie executives, but their helicopter crashed after being attacked by a tomacco-crazed sheep, destroying the last plant. Remarkably, the sheep survived the crash. In 2003, inspired by The Simpsons, Rob Baur from Lake Oswego, Oregon, successfully grafted a tomato plant onto the roots of a tobacco plant. This was possible because both plants belong to the Solanaceae (nightshade) family and are dicotyledons. Grafting monocotyledons is not feasible due to the scattered arrangement of their vascular tissues, which makes alignment impossible. The resulting plant produced fruit that resembled a normal tomato, but Baur suspected it contained lethal levels of nicotine, rendering it inedible. Subsequent testing confirmed that the plant's leaves contained some nicotine, but the first tomacco fruit, destroyed during testing, contained no nicotine. The second tomacco fruit was given to a Simpsons writer, the third was sold on eBay, and the fourth was consumed by a Xerox engineer, who reported no adverse effects. The tomacco plant continued to bear fruit until it died at 18 months of age due to weather-related causes, having spent the previous winter indoors. The process of creating tomacco was first described in a 1959 Scientific American article, which revealed that nicotine could be detected in tomato plants after grafting. Due to its significance in academic and industrial research, this article was reprinted in the 1968 Scientific American compilation Bio-Organic Chemistry. In 2004, the American Dialect Society humorously named tomacco the new word least likely to succeed.
